config.title: Write merge generic preserving key types

intro.title: Write merge generic preserving key types
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a `merge` function that combines two objects into one while preserving the original key types. You will learn how to use TypeScript generics to create a flexible function that works with any object shapes, ensuring the return type accurately reflects the merged keys. The core concept involves using generic type parameters to capture and combine the types of the input objects. You will work with TypeScript's object types and the spread operator to implement the merge logic. By the end, you will have a reusable, type-safe utility function for merging objects.
intro.usecase: This pattern is essential when building dashboard components that merge configuration objects from different sources while preserving type safety. For example, when creating a data visualization dashboard, you might need to merge default chart settings with user-customized options—ensuring properties like `colorScheme` or `dataKey` maintain their specific string literal types. Similarly, in form builders, merging field validation rules from templates with user-defined overrides requires preserving exact key types to prevent runtime errors. This technique ensures that merged objects retain their precise type information, which is crucial for autocomplete and type checking in complex applications.

objectives: Construct a generic function signature that accepts two distinct object types.
Apply intersection types to combine the keys and values from both input objects.
Implement a function body that merges two objects while preserving their original key types.
Initialize variables with the merged result to demonstrate type preservation.
Manipulate the generic constraints to ensure only object types are accepted.
Integrate the merge function into a TypeScript module for reuse.
Control the return type to explicitly reflect the combined structure of the inputs.

steps.instruction: Create a TypeScript file for the merge function. No external imports are needed for this lesson.
steps.hint: Simply create an empty TypeScript file. You can start with a comment indicating this is a TypeScript file.
steps.analogousExample:

// No imports needed for basic type operations
steps.seedCode:

steps.expectedOutcome: A clean TypeScript file is created, ready for implementing the merge function.
successCriteria: File is created with a TypeScript context comment and no imports.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a file, but make sure it's clearly a TypeScript file. Add a comment indicating this is for TypeScript code.
steps.feedbackWrong: This step requires creating a TypeScript file. Please create a file with a .ts extension or appropriate TypeScript context.

steps.title: Define the merge function signature with generics
steps.instruction: Define a function called 'merge' with two generic parameters T and U, taking parameters obj1 of type T and obj2 of type U. The function should return an object that combines both inputs.
steps.hint: Start with 'function merge<T, U>(obj1: T, obj2: U)' and add a return type annotation.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named 'merge' with two generic type parameters T and U, two parameters obj1 and obj2 with those types, and a return type that combines T and U.
successCriteria: The merge function is defined with generics T and U, parameters obj1: T and obj2: U, and a return type annotation.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure the function has two generic parameters (T and U) and two parameters with those types.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the function definition. It should be named 'merge', have two generic type parameters, and two parameters with those types.

steps.title: Add return type annotation to preserve key types
steps.instruction: Add a return type annotation of `T & U` to the merge function signature to indicate it returns an object containing all keys from both inputs.
steps.hint: After the parameter list, add a colon followed by `T & U` before the opening curly brace of the function body.
steps.expectedOutcome: The merge function signature includes a return type annotation `: T & U` to preserve the key types from both generic parameters.
successCriteria: The merge function has a return type annotation of `T & U` after the parameter list.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure to add the return type annotation `: T & U` right after the parameter list and before the function body.
steps.feedbackWrong: The return type annotation is missing or incorrect. Add `: T & U` after the parameter list to specify the intersection type.

steps.title: Implement the merge function body
steps.instruction: Inside the merge function, implement the body to return a new object that spreads both obj1 and obj2 using the spread operator.
steps.hint: Use the spread operator (...) to combine the properties of both objects into a new object.
steps.expectedOutcome: The merge function will now correctly combine two objects while preserving their key types.
successCriteria: The function body returns a new object created by spreading both obj1 and obj2.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using the spread operator (...) to combine both objects into a new object.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function body should return a new object that spreads both obj1 and obj2. Try using the spread operator: return { ...obj1, ...obj2 };

steps.title: Create test objects with different key types
steps.instruction: Below your merge function, create two test objects with different property names and types to use as inputs for testing.
steps.hint: Define two const variables with different keys and value types (e.g., string, number, boolean).
steps.expectedOutcome: Two const objects with distinct property names and types are defined, ready to be passed to merge.
successCriteria: Two const objects with different keys and types are created below the merge function.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created at least one object, but you need two with different property names and types.
steps.feedbackWrong: No test objects were created. Please define two const objects with different keys and value types.

steps.title: Call the merge function with test objects
steps.instruction: Call the merge function with your test objects and store the result in a variable named mergedResult.
steps.hint: Use the variable name mergedResult and pass your test objects as arguments to merge().
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: calling a function and storing the result
const result = addNumbers(5, 3);
steps.expectedOutcome: The merge function is called with concrete test objects, demonstrating how the generic types T and U are preserved in the return type.
successCriteria: The merge function is called with test objects and the result is stored in a variable named mergedResult.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're calling merge() with your test objects and storing the result in a variable named mergedResult.
steps.feedbackWrong: call the merge function with your test objects and store the result in a variable named mergedResult.

steps.title: Add type annotation to the result variable
steps.instruction: Add a type annotation to the result variable that explicitly shows the intersection type of the merged objects.
steps.hint: Use a colon followed by the type after the variable name. The type should combine the generic types T and U.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: typing a variable with an intersection type
const combined: { name: string } & { age: number } = { name: 'Alice', age: 30 };
steps.expectedOutcome: The result variable will have an explicit type annotation showing the combined types of objA and objB.
successCriteria: The result variable has a type annotation using the intersection type T & U.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the type annotation uses the intersection type T & U and follows the variable name with a colon.
steps.feedbackWrong: The type annotation is missing or incorrect. The result variable should have a type annotation that matches the intersection of the two generic types.

steps.title: Access properties from the merged result
steps.instruction: Access the 'name' property from the merged result and log it to the console.
steps.hint: Use dot notation on the result variable to access the property that came from objA.
steps.expectedOutcome: The 'name' property from objA is successfully accessed from the typed merged result, demonstrating type preservation.
successCriteria: The 'name' property is accessed from the result variable and logged to the console.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're accessing the 'name' property from the result variable and logging it with console.log.
steps.feedbackWrong: That's not quite right. Try accessing the 'name' property from the result variable and logging it to the console.

steps.title: Test with objects containing overlapping keys
steps.instruction: Create two new test objects with overlapping property names (e.g., both having a 'name' property) and call the merge function with them.
steps.hint: Define two objects where at least one property key appears in both objects. The second object's value will overwrite the first's in the merged result.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will see that when objects have overlapping keys, the merge function still works, and TypeScript correctly infers the intersection type, with the second object's property value taking precedence.
successCriteria: Two new objects with at least one overlapping property are defined, and the merge function is called with them.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure both objects have at least one property with the same name, and you call the merge function with them.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've created two objects with overlapping property names and called the merge function with them as arguments.

steps.title: Add console output to verify runtime behavior
steps.instruction: Add console.log statements to display the merged objects and their properties. Log the result variable and access its properties.
steps.hint: Use console.log with the result variable and its properties like result.name and result.age.
steps.expectedOutcome: The console will show the merged object and its individual properties, confirming the merge function works correctly at runtime.
successCriteria: Console.log statements display the result object and its name and age properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some console.log statements, but make sure to log both the result object and its individual properties (result.name and result.age).
steps.feedbackWrong: Console.log statements are missing or incorrect. Add statements to log the result variable and access its properties.
